scope: MEAS: Internet Archive metadata and file list (lp_messiaen-la-nativite-du-seigneur…, disc1/02.05), cached MP3 MD5 against the Archive manifest, envelope at 0.1–0.5 s, tuning offset and final-chord pitch, the Archive segmentation file and the end of the preceding track (The Wise Men). EXT: OCR of the Mercury MG 10069 sleeve, The American Organist October 1952 (OCR text), American Music Teacher November–December 1952 (OCR text), Wikipedia (La Nativité du Seigneur), Dame Gillian Weir’s programme note (Hollywood Bowl), Gowers’s King’s College booklet (timing only), a University of Houston student essay on the registration (used only as a pointer). Not an aural review.

corrections.finding: Section B and its cue stood at 143 s. The sound is near-silent from about 144.4 to 145.5 s and the loud passage starts at 145.6 s.
corrections.fix: Moved section B and its cue to 145 s.

corrections.finding: “A · Quieter opening” and “B · Full organ” misdescribe the audio. The track opens loudly: the first music (from about 1.9 s) rises to the same loudness as the later loud passage by 0:13–0:21 and drops at 22 s to a quiet stretch. Weir’s note and the Houston essay both describe full-organ chords and a descent of God at the start. The cue text said the organ “rises to full strength” at 143 s, which the first 20 s contradict.
corrections.fix: Labels now read “A · Loud opening, then quieter music” and “B · Sustained loud section”. The cue is retitled “Loud section begins” and says only that the organ becomes much louder and stays loud, apart from short dips, to the end.

corrections.finding: The intro, the dossier version field and the 372 s cue called the whole piece “the toccata”. Weir (“until a dazzling toccata signals the Incarnation”), Gowers (“the famous toccata at the end”) and the Houston essay (toccata in the last bars) place the toccata at the end of a longer piece.
corrections.fix: Intro and dossier now say the piece ends in a toccata; the 372 s cue says “this one” and “piece 9”. Weir added to the dossier sources.

corrections.finding: The evidence for the 0 s and 143 s cues ended with “Toccata after quieter pieces: Messiaen chapter on this site”, which supports no claim in either cue.
corrections.fix: Removed; the 145 s evidence now states what is heard.

checks.source: Item lists the track as VBR MP3, 07:08; the cached MP3 (md5 243f4a65…) matches the Archive manifest. The Archive file is 428.46 s. Metadata: publisher Mercury Classics, catalogue MG 10069, date 1952, collections album_recordings, vinyl_bostonpubliclibrary, audio_music, unlockedrecordings and a University of North Carolina Greensboro vinyl collection; no licence field and no litigation, restriction or dark marker.
checks.durationAndPitch: The music starts at about 1.9 s (about 1.3 s of the previous piece, a gap, then the opening chords) and ends at about 7:06; Gowers’s 2017 recording of the same piece lasts 9:32, so 7:08 is a brisk but ordinary length. Tuning: +32 cents against A = 440 Hz (A ≈ 448 Hz), steady across the track (concentration 0.78); the closing sonority is E and B at about +35 to +40 cents. No key is written in the file. The offset is a third of a semitone and cannot be separated into organ tuning and speed of recording or transfer; no semitone-scale discrepancy.
checks.identity: Sleeve: Mercury Classics MG 10069, “ERNEST WHITE playing the Memorial Hall Organ, Methuen, Mass.”, nine pieces in order, side B ends with “9. God among us”; recording “accomplished in August of 1949 under the engineering supervision of H. Vose Greenough”; organ history (Walcker 1857–62, Boston Music Hall 1863–84, Methuen 9 December 1909, G. Donald Harrison of Aeolian-Skinner). The Archive segmentation shows The Wise Men ending exactly where this track begins (890.892 s of the side-2 capture), so the track starts with the end of the previous piece and not with the first chord. Matrix numbers not shown.
checks.notes: Every cue checked against its source. 40 s, 200 s, 260 s, 320 s: sleeve text (history of the organ, Farnam and St Mary the Virgin, Greenough, preface “Emotion and sincerity above all!”, composition at 26 in Grenoble in summer 1935 per Wikipedia). 372 s: Wikipedia (première 27 February 1936 at La Trinité, Daniel-Lesur 1–3, Langlais 4–6, Grunenwald 7–9; Leduc Book IV for piece 9 alone). 400 s: The American Organist (“difficult-to-play and difficult-to-enjoy”; “If this work is one of your favorites, Mr. White should satisfy you completely”) and American Music Teacher (Mildred Andrews, University of Oklahoma: “a musical architect of real genius”). 0 s: preface point (2), “the living, sorrowing God in our midst (9th and 7th pieces)”, and the epigraph (Ecclesiasticus 24; John 1:14; Luke 1:46–47). The one audio-feature cue (145 s) is confirmed by the envelope. Eight notes for 428.5 s (limit 11). Voice rules read by hand: no closing lines, personification, antithesis, triplets or colon reveals; the one colon introduces the list of three organists.

rights.decision: Publish on the territorial EU basis stated in the dossier; US status is not claimed.
rights.reasoning: (1) First publication: The American Organist, October 1952 (vol. 35, no. 10) reviews “Ernest White, Methuen Memorial Hall, Mass.… Mercury 12” lp. MG-10069, $4.85”, and American Music Teacher, November–December 1952 reviews the same record, so the LP was on sale by autumn 1952 (the first-issue date may be earlier). A phonogram published in 1952 had run its 50-year EU term by the end of 2002 and was not revived by Directive 2011/77/EU. (2) Provenance: a studio-quality LP of a session in August 1949 issued by Mercury Classics, scanned with its own sleeve; neither a live nor a broadcast capture, and no re-labelling. (3) Composition: Messiaen died in 1992, so the work is in copyright in the EU until the end of 2062; the dossier states this and the page does not claim otherwise. (4) The Internet Archive item carries no licence and no litigation or restriction marker.
rights.limits: The Archive’s date field (1952) is the issue year, not the session year.

observations.finding: Weir’s note gives an order of events (descent of God, a few serene bars, increasing intensity, then the toccata) and the Houston essay gives a bar-level outline, but neither can be tied to times in this recording without the score, so no cue was added.
